full_judgment:
2. After placing the petition and impugned Judgment learned Advocate for the petitioner submitted that respondent No. 1 member, Labour Appellate Tribunal acted illegally in passing the impugned Judgment holding that terms of a terminated settlement cannot by interpretation be held to be operative. He further submitted that respondent No. I instead of interpreting the terms of the terminated settlement interpreted sub-section (2) of section 40 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance which was not the prayer of respondent No.2. He further submitted that application of the respondent No. 2 was beyond the scope of section 50 of the Industrial Relations Ordinance. He further submitted that respondent No. 2 failed to consider that after termination of the settlement the same has no force and, as such, acted illegally in passing the impugned judgment. 

 3. Learned Advocate for the respondent Nos. 2 and 3 after placing the affidavit-in-opposition submitted that respondent No.1 did not commit any illegality in holding that annulments and benefits of the workers at the previous rates will continue till new settlement is arrived at mutually on fresh terms and conditions and for that parties may negotiate on the basis of charter of demands already submitted by the respondent No. 2 to the management. He further submitted that terms and conditions of the service once effective cannot be altered to the detriment of the employees as the same may lead to Industrial unrest. He further submitted that termination of a settlement does not absolve the parties from the obligations under the same but gives them opportunity to enter into a new settlement by negotiation and agreement between the parties failing which the dispute is to be settled by an award of the Labour Court. 

 4. It appears that respondent No. 2 entered into various settlements with the petitioner in respect of the service conditions and wages of the workers from time to time and last settlement was arrived that on 4-4-95. Petitioner terminated the said settlement by two months’ notice dated 19-3-98 as per the provision of section 40(2) of the said Ordinance which was effective from 19-5-98. Thereafter, the respondent No. 2 placed before the petitioner a charter of demands on 20-5-98 under section 26 of the said Ordinance claiming certain higher rates of emoluments and benefits over the rates which were being enjoined by the workers. Petitioner by notice dated 8-6-98 modified the previous rates of emoluments and benefits and declared much lower rates in comparison with the existing rates. Thereafter by letter dated 9-6-98 respondent No. 2 protested against the said notice of the petitioner. Thereafter respondent Nos. 2 and 3 filed Interpretation Case No. 30 of 98 before the respondent No. 1. 

 5. The case was contested by the petitioner by filing written objection denying the allegations and asserting that the petition was beyond the scope of section 50 of said Ordinance and that a terminated settlement cannot be interpreted and petitioner is at liberty to reduce emoluments and benefits of the workers after the termination of the settlement which was no longer binding upon the petitioner. 

 7. There is no dispute between the parties that the petitioner entered into settlement with the respondent No. 2 Workers Union on 22-2-86, 12-8- 86, 14-7-90, 19-11-90,22-12-92 and lastly, on 4-4-95. There is also no dispute that the petitioner by notice dated 19-3-98 terminated settlement dated 4- 4-95 and thereafter on 20-5-98 respondent No.2 submitted a charter of demands claiming the higher rates of emoluments and benefits over the rates agreed on 4-4-95. Instead of agreeing to the charter of demands petitioner issued notice dated 8-6-98 by which previous rates of emoluments and benefits were much reduced. In such circumstances terminated settlement dated 4-4-95 case for interpretation before the respondent No.1 in, Interpretation Case No. 30 of 98. A Division Bench of the then Dhaka High Court in the case of Pakistan Tobacco Company Limited vs Chairman Second Labour Court after considering the provisions of section 19(6) of the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 applicable in India and provision of section 40(2) of the Industrial Relations Ordinance almost in the same language and also relying on the decision of the Bombay High Court under the Industrial Disputes Act 1947 reported in (1957) 2 LV 256, Supreme Court of India reported in AIR 1957 (SC) 38, Supreme Court of Pakistan reported in PLD 1961 (SC) 393 held as follows: 

 "Therefore what the law provides by section 40(2) of the Ordinance is that by expressing its intention not to be bound by the award or the settlement after the period of expiry, any of the parties to the settlement is at liberty to negotiate the terms which was the subject matter of the settlement but it does not mean that the rights and obligations arising out of the settlement or rights and obligations flowing therefrom are wiped out. It is equally not permissible for any of the parties to the settlement by merely expressing its intention unilaterally not to be bound by the settlement arrived at between them. It only means that the parties of the settlement are at liberty to negotiate the terms which were not negotiable during the operation of the settlement." 

 "After expiry of the specific period contractually or statutorily fixed as the period of operation of an award or settlement, the same does not become non-est but continues to be binding. Law abhors vacuum. Until a new contract or award replaces the previous one the former settlement or award will regulate the relation between the parties. The precedents on the point, the principles of Industrial Law, the constitutional sympathy of part IV and the sound rules, of statutory construction converge to the same conclusion. "Considering the latest decision of the Indian Supreme Court along with aforesaid decision of the Dhaka High Court respondent No.1 held as follows: 

 "With regard to the points raised that the service of notice by opposite party management on fixing the emoluments and benefits at a rate much lower with the rate enjoyed by workers as per earlier settlement and being not commensurate with the present market price level and cost of living I am of the view the emoluments and benefits of the workers at the previous rates will continue and have its binding force till new settlement is arrived at mutually on fresh terms and conditions and for that the parties may negotiate on the basis of charter of demand already submitted by the employees union to the management." 

 9. Industrial Relations Ordinance 1969 was promulgated to regulate mutual relationship between the employers and workers. Intention of the said law is to maintain industrial peace to avoid lockout and strike. The said law provides for raising industrial dispute by either party and for arriving at settlement by negotiation between the employers and the workers Union which is the collective bargaining agent and failing any settlement regarding an industrial dispute Labour Court has been empowered to give award regarding the industrial dispute. Thus the intention of the said law is that settlement or award must be complied with by the parties. Sub-section (2) of section 40 provides that a settlement shall be binding for the agreed period upon the parties and in the absence of any such agreement for a period of one year from the date of signing the same and shall continue to be binding on the parties even after the expiry of the aforesaid period until it is terminated by two months’ notice. 

 10. Now the question is whether after termination of a settlement rights and obligations created under the terminated settlement can be disregarded by either party of the settlement. In the Dhaka High Court case referred to herein above the court opined that the terms of the terminated settlement are binding on the workers. On the other hand, in the Indian Supreme Court decision of 1980 it was held that terms of the terminated settlement is binding on the employers. The ratio decidendi of the aforesaid two decisions has been followed by the respondent No.1 in passing the impugned judgment considering the intention of the legislature to avoid industrial unrest and to maintain harmony in the industrial field. We find no illegality in such interpretation holding that the rights and obligations under the terminated settlement shall remain operative till a new settlement is arrived at between the parties or an award is given by the Labour Court. 

 11. We find no merit in the contention that a terminated settlement cannot be interpreted under the provisions of section 50 of the said Ordinance. We also do not agree with the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that with the termination of the settlement petitioner is at liberty not to follow the terms of such settlement. Interpretation put by the respondent No. 1 on the terminated settlement necessarily involved interpretation of section 40(2) of the said Ordinance. But that does not mean that, respondent No. 1 merely interpreted section 40(2) of the said Ordinance instead of interpreting the terminated settlement which has no existence. Terms of the terminated settlement creating rights and obligations shall continue to be effective till a new settlement is arrived at or an award is given by the Labour Court. 

 12. Section 7 of the Payment of Wages Act 1936 provides that wages of employed persons shall be paid to him without deduction of any kind except those authorized by or under that Act. Thus it is clear that the employer cannot reduce the wages of the workers even after termination of a settlement until a new settlement is arrived at or award is given by the Labour Court on the failure of the employer and the collective bargaining agent of the workers to arrive at a settlement to avoid industrial unrest and to maintain industrial peace in the larger interest of the society.
